limitations_and_boundaries: The link between cell polarity and the Hippo pathway may be indirect; some proteins like Fat may regulate polarity and Hippo via different mechanisms.
Mammalian Fat orthologs do not seem to be major regulators of the Hippo pathway.
Discrepancies in EGF/insulin regulation of YAP may be due to differences in experimental settings or cell types.
YAP is not required for development and normal homeostasis of some tissues (e.g., mammary glands, intestine) but is critical for regeneration after damage.

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP/TAZ are regulated by cell-cell contact, which is the first discovered signal regulating the Hippo pathway.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: Cell-cell contact was discovered as the first signal regulating the Hippo pathway (Zhao et al., 2007).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP/TAZ are regulated by cell attachment to ECM, and that constitutively active YAP promotes survival of detached cells.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: YAP is activated during the process of cell attachment but inactivated when cells are detached (Zhao et al., 2012). Expression of constitutively active YAP promotes survival of detached cells, suggesting that cancer cells with high YAP activity may escape anoikis and undergo metastasis.

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that the Hippo pathway is regulated by negative feedback loops in both Drosophila and mammals.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: In Drosophila, regulation of the Hippo pathway is fine-tuned by a built-in negative-feedback loop in which activation of Yki turns on the expression of upstream regulators, including Four-jointed, Ex, Mer, Kibra, and Wts (Cho et al., 2006; Genevet et al., 2010; Hamaratoglu et al., 2006; Jukam et al., 2013). Consistently, a similar negative feedback mechanism also exists in mammalian cells.

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP/TAZ are critical for early embryonic development, including the first cell fate specification in preimplantation embryos.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: YAP/TAZ are critical during early embryonic development. Although TAZ knockout mice are viable, YAP knockout mice die at E8.5, and blastomeres stop dividing before the morula (16–32 cells) stage when YAP and TAZ are both deleted (Hossain et al., 2007; Makita et al., 2008; Morin-Kensicki et al., 2006; Nishioka et al., 2009; Tian et al., 2007).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP/TAZ are regulated by the actin cytoskeleton and Rho GTPases, which integrate upstream signals.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: The actin cytoskeleton and Rho GTPases are not only important in maintaining cell morphology, but also play important roles in regulating cell proliferation and differentiation (Jaffe and Hall, 2005). Manipulation of the actin cytoskeleton, such as overexpression of Rho GTPases or inhibition of Rho by C3 toxin, dramatically modulates YAP/TAZ activity (Dupont et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2012).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP/TAZ are regulated by hypoxia via HIF1 and SIAH1/2.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: Under hypoxic conditions, the hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF1) stimulates expression of SIAH1/2, two E3 ubiquitin ligases. SIAH1/2 then promote ubiquitination and degradation of LATS2, leading to YAP/TAZ activation (Ma et al., 2015; Xiang et al., 2014) (Figure 3).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP/TAZ are regulated by Wnt signaling through multiple mechanisms.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: YAP/TAZ have been shown to be components of the destruction complex and are regulated by Wnt in a fashion similar to that of b-catenin (Azzolin et al., 2012, 2014). However, a recent study suggests that Wnt activates YAP/TAZ via Frizzled (a GPCR-like Wnt receptor), Ga12/13, Rho GTPases, and LATS1/2 (Park et al., 2015).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP/TAZ are involved in drug resistance and cancer relapse.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: YAP/TAZ activity is also linked to drug resistance and cancer relapse. Cultured breast cancer cells with high YAP/TAZ activity show resistance to drugs such as taxol, 5-fluorouracil, and doxorubicin (Cordenonsi et al., 2011; Lai et al., 2011; Touil et al., 2014).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that YAP may play a tumor-suppressor role in hematological cancers.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: in contrast to its oncogenic function in most solid tumors, YAP seems to play a tumor-suppressor role in hematological cancers. The YAP gene locus is frequently deleted in hematological cancer, and expression of YAP or inhibition of MST1 leads to growth inhibition and increased apoptosis (Cottini et al., 2014).

missed_core_items.description: The extraction omits the core finding that the Hippo pathway can be therapeutically targeted, including inhibitors for MST1/2, LATS1/2, and YAP-TEAD interaction.
missed_core_items.source_excerpt: The core Hippo pathway is a kinase cascade, and protein kinases are usually druggable. Thus, inhibitors for MAP4K4, MST1/2, or LATS1/2 may be developed to induce YAP/TAZ activity and facilitate the process of wound healing, tissue repair, or regeneration and possibly for treating degenerative diseases (Figure 4).

evidence_spans.content: Activation of YAP by transgenic expression or deletion of upstream regulators results in expansion of progenitor cells, impaired differentiation, and hyperplasia in intestine, liver, skin, and nervous system.

experiments_or_tasks: Tissue-specific deletion of Yap causes abnormalities in heart, skin, kidney; but not in mammary glands or intestine under normal conditions.
YAP is critical for tissue regeneration after damage (e.g., intestine after DSS colitis, liver after partial hepatectomy, neonatal heart).
YAP is highly nuclear in stem/progenitor cells of multiple tissues (e.g., intestine, liver, skin).

methods.name: Regeneration assay

Mammalian orthologs: MST1/2 (Hpo), SAV1 (Sav), LATS1/2 (Wts), MOB1a/b (Mats), YAP/TAZ (Yki).
YAP/TAZ and Yki are key effectors; they bind TEAD transcription factors to regulate gene expression.

methods.name: Genetic deletion and overexpression
